summary: Introduces an in-band way for DNS operators to publish authenticated information about zones they serve. It lets managed DNS operators securely announce DNSSEC key parameters, even when no DS records exist yet, so the parent can set up the delegation. It updates RFC 7344 and RFC 8078.

plainLanguage.summary: To turn on DNSSEC for a domain, the registry that runs the parent zone needs the domain's signing key, and it needs to be sure that key really belongs to the domain. This document lets the company that hosts the domain publish a signed copy of that key in a place the registry can check. The registry compares the two copies and only then writes the record that makes the domain signed.

subtitle: How a DNS operator can publish signed hints that let a parent zone safely switch on DNSSEC for a new delegation.

tldr.problem: A parent zone cannot sign a delegation to a child zone until it has the child's DNSSEC key in a form it can trust. The keys are usually passed by hand, which is slow and error-prone, and the automated alternative in RFC 8078 has no way to check the keys when the delegation has no chain of trust yet.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9615 lets the child DNS operator copy the CDS and CDNSKEY records to a signaling name under a _signal domain built from the child's own nameserver names, and sign them with the signaling zone's key. The parental agent then compares those signed records with the ones at the child apex and only publishes the DS record when they match exactly.
tldr.outcome: The parent's checks are cryptographic rather than a delay, so the procedure is strictly stronger than the Accept after Delay method of RFC 8078. The document updates RFC 7344 and RFC 8078, and IANA has registered the _signal node name for CDS and CDNSKEY.

today: RFC 9615 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2024, and it has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 7344 and RFC 8078, and IANA has added the entry _signal to the registry of underscored and globally scoped DNS node names for both CDS and CDNSKEY records.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Securing a DNS delegation for the first time requires the child's DNSSEC parameters to be conveyed to the parent through some trusted channel. The communication has to happen between the parent registry and the DNSSEC key holder, and what that means in practice depends on the relationship the child has with the parent. The key is usually held by the child DNS operator, and the registrar, possibly through the registrant, may also be involved.

As observed in RFC 7344, these dependencies often result in a manual process that is susceptible to mistakes and errors, and because of the annoyance of the process, the parties involved may avoid getting a DS record published at all.

Automated provisioning of DS records was specified in RFC 8078. It is based on the parental agent, which is the registry or registrar, fetching DNSSEC key parameters from the CDS and CDNSKEY records at the child zone's apex and validating them somehow. The child's existing DNSSEC chain of trust can be used for that validation when the aim is to update an existing DS record set, such as during a key rollover. When a delegation is being bootstrapped, the child zone has no existing validation path, so other means of establishing that the records are legitimate have to be found.

Because there has been no complete solution built into the DNS itself, either out-of-band methods have been used to complete the chain of trust, or cryptographic validation has been dropped in favour of weaker cross-checks such as Accept after Delay. This document closes that gap. It introduces an in-band method for DNS operators to publish information about the zones they are authoritative for, in an authenticated manner and on a per-zone basis, so a managed DNS operator can securely announce the DNSSEC key parameters for the zones it manages. The parent can then use that signal to validate the CDS and CDNSKEY records at an insecure child zone's apex and, on success, secure the delegation.

The mechanism does not cover some edge cases, such as excessively long child zone names or domains whose nameservers are all inside the domain itself. DNSSEC bootstrapping is one application of the generic signaling mechanism the document specifies; other applications, such as publishing operational metadata or API endpoints, may follow.
sections.plainLanguage: A parent zone hands a domain over to a child zone. To make that handover secure, the parent needs the child's signing key and has to be sure the key really belongs to that child. The key is usually passed by hand, which is slow and easy to get wrong. This document replaces that hand-off with a check the parent can do by itself: the hosting company signs the key information and publishes it where the parent can verify the signature.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
The document names the roles in the exchange. The child is the zone being delegated and the parent is the zone that holds the delegation. The child DNS operator is the entity that maintains and publishes the zone information for the child DNS, and the parental agent is the entity with the authority to insert DS records into the parent zone on behalf of the child, which could be the registry, the registrar, a reseller or some other authorized entity.

The four signaling terms describe where the child publishes its signal. A signaling domain is a domain name constructed by prepending the label _signal to a hostname taken from a delegation's NS record set, so there are as many signaling domains as there are distinct NS targets. A signaling name is the label prefixed to a signaling domain to identify a signaling type and a child zone's name. A signaling record is a DNS record located at a signaling name under a signaling domain, used by the child DNS operator to publish information about the child. A signaling type is a signal type identifier, such as _dsboot for DNSSEC bootstrapping. The signaling zone is the zone that is authoritative for a given signaling record.
sections.plainLanguage: Several names are used for the pieces of the exchange. The child DNS operator is the company that hosts the domain and publishes its DNS records. The parental agent is the registry or registrar that writes records into the parent zone. A signaling domain is a special name built by adding the label _signal to one of the domain's own nameserver hostnames, and a signaling name adds one more label to say which kind of signal it is.

sections.title: The Signaling Mechanism
sections.content:
The mechanism is general: a child DNS operator publishes an authenticated signal about a child zone, and parental agents or other parties discover and process it. Authenticity comes from ordinary DNSSEC validation.

Each signaling zone must be signed and must be validatable by the parental agent, which means it must have a valid, publicly resolvable DNSSEC chain of trust. This is typically achieved by securely delegating each signaling zone. For example, when publishing a signal about a child zone whose NS records are ns1.example.net and ns2.example.org, the child DNS operator must make sure the parental agent has a valid chain of trust for the zones authoritative for the signaling domains _signal.ns1.example.net and _signal.ns2.example.org.

To publish information about the child zone in an authenticated fashion, the child DNS operator must publish one or more signaling records at a signaling name under each signaling domain. The signaling records must be accompanied by RRSIG records created with the key of the corresponding signaling zone, and their type and contents depend on the type of signal.

The signaling name identifies the child and the signaling type. It is the child name with the final root label removed, prefixed with a label containing the signaling type.
sections.plainLanguage: The mechanism has two halves. The child publishes a copy of its key information under a special name and signs that copy with the key of the zone where the special name lives. The parent then resolves that name and checks the signature in the normal way, so the parent learns the key from a source it can verify rather than from a message someone sent it.

sections.title: Publishing the Consent Signal
sections.content:
To confirm its willingness to act as the child's delegated signer and to authenticate the child's CDS and CDNSKEY record sets, the child DNS operator must copy those records to the corresponding signaling name under each signaling domain, excluding the signaling domains that fall within the child domain itself. For simplicity the operator may also copy them to signaling domains inside the child domain, although those are not used for validation.

Unlike the CDS and CDNSKEY records at the child's apex, a signaling record set must be signed with the key of the corresponding signaling zone, and its contents must be identical to the record set published at the child's apex.

Existing use of CDS and CDNSKEY records was specified at the child apex only. This protocol extends the use of these record types to owner names other than the apex, for the purpose of DNSSEC bootstrapping. To exclude the possibility of a semantic collision, there must not be a zone cut at a signaling name.

The worked example bootstraps the child zone example.co.uk, whose NS records are ns1.example.net, ns2.example.org and ns3.example.co.uk. The required signaling domains are _signal.ns1.example.net and _signal.ns2.example.org, and the operator authenticates the CDS and CDNSKEY records found at the child's apex by copying them as CDS and CDNSKEY records at the names _dsboot.example.co.uk._signal.ns1.example.net and _dsboot.example.co.uk._signal.ns2.example.org. These record sets are signed with DNSSEC just like any other zone data. Publication under the in-domain name _signal.ns3.example.co.uk is not required.
sections.plainLanguage: The child publishes the same key records in two places. At the top of its own domain they are signed by the domain itself, which the parent cannot yet check. At the signaling name they are signed by the zone that holds the signal, which the parent can check. The contents of the two copies must be identical, so the parent can compare them.

sections.title: Validating CDS and CDNSKEY Records
sections.content:
To validate a child's CDS and CDNSKEY record set for DNSSEC bootstrapping, the parental agent, knowing both the child zone name and its NS hostnames, must carry out four steps.

In step 1 it verifies that the child has no DS records published at the parent and that at least one of its nameservers is outside the child domain. In step 2 it queries the CDS and CDNSKEY record set at the child zone apex directly from each of the authoritative servers given by the delegation's parent-side NS record set, without caching. In step 3 it queries the CDS and CDNSKEY record set located at the signaling name under each signaling domain, except those inside the child domain, using a trusted DNS resolver and enforcing DNSSEC validation. In step 4 it checks, separately by record type, that all the record sets retrieved in steps 2 and 3 have equal contents.

If the steps succeed without error, the record sets are verified and the parental agent can proceed with the publication of the DS record set under the precautions described in Section 5 of RFC 8078. The agent must abort if an error occurs: in step 1 if the child is already securely delegated or has in-domain nameservers only; in step 2 on any failure to retrieve the record set at the child apex from any of the authoritative nameservers; in step 3 on any failure to retrieve the record sets at the signaling name under any signaling domain, including a failure of DNSSEC validation or unauthenticated data, shown by the AD bit not being set; and in step 4 on inconsistent responses, including a record set that is empty in one of steps 2 or 3 but not the other.

In-domain signaling names have no chain of trust at bootstrapping time, so the parental agent does not consider them during validation. Consequently, if all NS hostnames are in-domain, validation cannot be completed and no DS records are published. The same follows from the length limits on DNS names: fully qualified signaling names must be valid DNS names, so the protocol does not work for unusually long child domain names or NS hostnames. As a workaround, an out-of-domain nameserver can be added to the initial NS record set and removed once bootstrapping is complete, with automation for this available through CSYNC records.
sections.plainLanguage: The parent checks the signal in four steps. It first confirms that the domain is not yet signed and that at least one nameserver sits outside the domain. It then fetches the key records straight from the domain's own servers, fetches the signed copy from the signaling name, and compares the two sets of records. If anything fails, or if the two sets differ even in one record, the parent stops and does not sign the delegation.

sections.title: Triggers and Discovery
sections.content:
Parental agents should start the procedure once one of the following conditions is met: the agent receives a new or updated NS record set for a child; it receives a notification that the child wishes to have its CDS or CDNSKEY record set processed; it encounters a signaling record during a proactive, opportunistic scan, such as daily queries of signaling records for some or all of its delegations; it encounters a signaling record during an NSEC walk or when parsing a signaling zone, for example when the zone is made available by zone transfer from the child DNS operator; or any other condition deemed appropriate by local policy.

Timer-based triggers such as scans have undesirable properties for processing delay and scaling, so on-demand triggers such as notifications are preferable. Using them reduces both the delay and the amount of scanning traffic.

Most discovery methods, such as daily scans of delegations, are based directly on the delegation's NS record set, and those NS names can be used as they are by the bootstrapping procedure. Some discovery methods do not give reliable knowledge of the delegation's NS record set. When signaling names are discovered by an NSEC walk or a zone transfer of a signaling zone, the parental agent must not assume that a nameserver under whose signaling domain a signaling record appears is actually authoritative for the corresponding child. Whenever a list of bootstrappable domains is obtained by any means other than directly from the parent, the agent must ascertain that the delegation actually contains the nameserver hostname seen during discovery, and must ensure that signaling-record queries are only made against the proper set of nameservers listed in the child's delegation from the parent.
sections.plainLanguage: The parent can start the check when a domain asks it to, when it notices a change to a delegation, or on a schedule. Pushing the request is faster and produces less traffic than scanning every domain every day. One caution applies to any way of finding domains other than reading the parent zone: a nameserver whose name appears in a signal is not proof that it serves that domain, so the parent must check the delegation first and query only the nameservers the delegation lists.

sections.title: Operational Recommendations
sections.content:
For the child DNS operator, it is possible to add CDS and CDNSKEY records and the matching signaling records to a zone without the domain owner's explicit knowledge. To spare domain owners from being caught off guard by the DS changes that follow, operators following this practice are advised to make it transparent, for example by informing the domain owner during zone creation or by notifying them by email.

When a zone is transferred to another DNS operator, the old and new operators need to cooperate to achieve a smooth transition, for example by using the multi-signer protocols of RFC 8901. If all else fails, the domain owner might have to ask for the removal of all DS records and have the transfer performed insecurely.

Signaling domains should be delegated as standalone zones, so that the apex of the signaling zone coincides with the signaling domain. It is permissible for the signaling domain to sit inside a signaling zone with fewer labels, but a zone cut ensures that bootstrapping does not require changes to the zone that holds the nameserver hostname.

Once the operator knows that particular signaling record sets have been processed, for example because the result is visible in the parent zone, it is advised to remove them. That reduces the size of the signaling zone and makes bulk processing more efficient.

For the parental agent, stalemate situations caused by a mismatch of stale cached records have to be avoided if DNSSEC bootstrapping is to be timely. Queries into signaling domains should therefore be made with an initially empty resolver cache, or by some other method that retrieves fresh data from the authoritative servers. It is also recommended that QNAME minimization from RFC 9156 be used when resolving queries for signaling records, to guard against certain attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The hosting company is advised to tell the domain owner before it adds the records, to hand over cleanly when the domain moves to another host, to give each signaling domain its own zone, and to delete the signal once it has been used. The registry is advised not to answer from its cache when it fetches a signal, because an old cached answer and a new one may disagree and stall the process.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The method introduced here is based on the approaches in Section 3 of RFC 8078 but adds authentication to the CDS and CDNSKEY concept. Its security level is therefore strictly higher than that of the existing approaches described in that document, such as Accept after Delay. Apart from this general improvement, the same security considerations apply as in RFC 8078.

The level of rigor required in the validation procedure is needed to prevent the publication of an ill-conceived DS record set that is authorized only under a subset of the NS hostnames. This ensures, for example, that an operator in a multihomed setup cannot enable DNSSEC unless the other operators agree.

In any case, the child DNS operator has authoritative knowledge of the child's CDS and CDNSKEY records, so it can readily detect fraudulent provisioning of DS records.

To prevent the parents of nameserver hostnames from becoming a single point of failure for a delegation, both in resolution availability and in the trust model of the protocol, it is advisable to diversify the path from the root to the child's nameserver hostnames, for example by using different and independently operated top-level domains for each of them.

If QNAME minimization is not used when querying for signaling records, an upstream parent of a signaling domain will see those CDS and CDNSKEY queries and could respond with an authoritative answer signed with its own key instead of sending the referral. Enabling QNAME minimization reduces the attack surface for such a forgery.
sections.plainLanguage: The check is stronger than the older methods, which relied on waiting rather than on verifying anything. The strict comparison also stops one operator in a shared setup from signing a domain that other operators have not agreed to. Two operational points follow: the domain's nameservers should not all sit under one top-level domain, so that one failure cannot stop the delegation, and the lookup for the signal should be made in a way that does not reveal the full name to every server on the way.

The four steps the parental agent must complete

items.title: Step 1, not secure yet
items.text: Check that the child has no DS records at the parent and that at least one of its nameservers is outside the child domain.

items.title: Step 2, ask the child
items.text: Query the CDS and CDNSKEY records at the child apex directly from each authoritative server, without caching.

items.title: Step 3, ask the signal
items.text: Query the signaling name under each signaling domain with a trusted resolver and enforce DNSSEC validation.

items.title: Step 4, compare
items.text: Check that the records retrieved in steps 2 and 3 are equal, separately for each record type.
